units.text: A. Four tools for not confusing story with law
1. Simplicity of the rule is not simplicity of the world

A complete computational explanation must specify at least the rule, initial state and how the result relates to observation. A program of a few characters displaying a huge file does not explain that file through a few characters: the information has been stored elsewhere. This elementary example shows why ‘can a few rules produce the universe?’ must be accompanied by ‘what have we already put into the initial conditions?’

We can compare two explanations of the same sequence. The first says ‘read the next entry in this table’, and the table contains all results. The second offers a short rule and short initial state from which results can be generated. Both reproduce the past; the second compresses information more. Yet past compression alone does not guarantee future prediction. We need testing on data unused in choosing the rule.

The same caution applies to emergence. If we already hide in the generator the complex structure we wish to explain, we have not explained its appearance. If a robust structure appears across many initial conditions and a class of mechanisms, we have better reason to speak of an emergent regularity. Robustness must be measured, not suggested by a spectacular animation.
2. A provable limit to simulation detection

Let S denote a precise simulated-world model and N a precise competing model we call nonsimulated. D is an observable event and E an experiment accessible to the observer. Assume the models give the same observation distribution: for every permitted experiment and every event D, they assign the same probability:
P(D | S, E) = P(D | N, E).

For any event with nonzero probability, the likelihood ratio is then 1. Those data favor neither model over the other. If we begin with different preferences, they may remain different, but this experiment has not made them better supported.

Adaptive experimental choice does not help either if equality holds after every possible observation history. The probability of an outcome sequence is obtained by multiplying successive conditional probabilities. If every factor agrees between models, so does the product. The adaptive strategy therefore produces the same distribution of observable histories. This is an elementary proof of indistinguishability under the stated conditions, not a claim that every simulation is undetectable.

The way out is not a miraculous statistical method. We must find an experiment for which equality’s premises no longer hold, acquire a new channel or restrict the model class. Creative research can begin here. The clear limit shows where the difference must be sought.
3. Why a spectacular result does not eliminate alternatives

Invent two models, A and B. Before a test, assign A a probability of 1% and B the remaining 99%. Assume, strictly for this example, no other possibilities exist. An outcome D is ten times more probable under A than B. The initial A:B odds were 1:99. After the outcome they become 10:99, so A’s probability reaches approximately 9.2%, not certainty.

The calculation does not establish what probability should be assigned to simulation. The numbers are chosen only to show the difference between ‘the data favor a model’ and ‘the model is now almost certain’. A real problem requires justifying both observation probabilities under models and treatment of alternatives. A vague model that does not say how probable D is cannot receive a numerical advantage merely because the outcome can be narrated in its vocabulary.

If the observer searched hundreds of possible outcomes and chose the one favoring A, even the ten-to-one ratio cannot be accepted without examining selection. Data must be analyzed alongside the procedure by which they were sought and selected. Arithmetic precision does not repair a poorly defined comparison.
4. The profile of a purported law

A useful profile begins with the exact statement and domain: which objects, scales and conditions? It continues with observable quantities, units and measurement procedure. It includes error tolerance, auxiliary assumptions and the difference between an exact relationship in the model and an approximation in application. These few details are worth more than an unexplained adjective ‘universal’.

The second part records support: what was measured, derived or merely assumed? Which new prediction succeeded? Which laboratory or independent method verified it? What result would seriously weaken confidence? When such a result appears, we explain why we revise the law, conditions or instrument; we do not automatically choose whichever option preserves the author’s authority.

The third part examines transfer and social power. Was the relationship tested in the context where it is now used? Is it a physical constraint or an institution-dependent regularity? Who gains resources, prestige or impunity through this formulation? Who bears an error’s cost? These questions do not decide whether the law is true, but clarify why it deserves independent testing.

The final field separates descriptive from normative conclusions. ‘Under conditions C, behavior X produces outcome Y’ does not mean ‘we must preserve C’ or ‘Y is good’. A law may show how an effect is obtained; choosing the effect and allocating costs require additional arguments. This is the minimal discipline by which law remains a tool of knowledge rather than a command to stop thinking.
